 BREAKING: Alabama state Rep. Patrick Sellers indicted on 4 counts of wire fraud Alabama state Rep. Patrick Sellers indicted on 4 counts of wire fraud 
 Federal prosecutors allege he fraudulently obtained more than $240,000 in COVID-19 relief money and used it for personal benefit 
 State Rep. Patrick Sellers indicted By Morgan Hightower Published : Nov. 19, 2026 at 9:42 AM CST | Updated : seconds ago Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google BIRMINGHAM, Ala. ( WBRC ) - A federal grand jury has indicted Alabama State Rep. Patrick Sellers on four counts of wire fraud, accusing him of fraudulently getting more than $240,000 in COVID-19 relief money and using it for his own personal benefit.
 Sellers, a Democrat from Pleasant Grove, has represented House District 57 since November 2022. He is also pastor of Mount Zion Missionary Baptist Church in Birmingham.
 According to the indictment, the alleged fraud took place between July 2020 and May 2021, before Sellers took office and while he was working as the Chief of Staff for the President of the Alabama State Missionary Baptist Convention (ASMBC). 
 During a news conference announcing the indictment, U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Alabama Phil Williams said, “This is certainly not all the evidence. This is a very robust indictment, and certainly would be a robust trial.”
 Williams said each count carries up to 20 years in federal prison.
 When reached for comment, Sellers’ attorney, Matt Hart, said, “It’s notable that none of the allegations against Representative Sellers assert any use or abuse of his official position. However, the Government’s case is still emerging and we will have no comment until we’ve had the opportunity to understand the charges and the evidence.”
 What the indictment alleges 
 The indictment unsealed Thursday following his arrest alleges that Sellers solicited grants and loans through the U.S. Small Business Administration, the State of Alabama, and an Alabama nonprofit on behalf of the ASMBC 501(c)(3), Project Zion, Inc., and Sellers Lawn Care, described as “a fictitious business entity.”
 Instead of using the money received for the benefit of the non-profits, federal prosecutors said that Sellers spent a “large” portion of the money on personal credit card payments, mortgage payments on his home, water bills, loan payments, and his daughters’ college tuition.
 According to the indictment, Sellers received:
 ASMBC 501(c)(3): A $20,000 SBA Economic Injury Disaster Loan (EIDL), a $15,000 state nonprofit relief grant, a $20,000 state Revive Plus grant and a $50,000 grant from a nonprofit. 
 Project Zion: A $44,900 EIDL, a $20,000 state Revive Plus grant and a $50,000 grant from a nonprofit. 
 Sellers Lawn Care: A $20,415 Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loan. 
 According to the indictment, the alleged conduct took place between July 2020 and May 2021, before Sellers took office. (House of Representatives) ASMBC 501(c)(3) 
 Prosecutors allege Sellers took control of the ASMBC 501(c)(3) in 2019 by setting up a bank account under that name that listed his home address in Pleasant Grove instead of the non-profit’s in Selma, creating a new email account for the non-profit, and the nonprofit’s mailing address with the IRS was changed from the Selma headquarters to his home.
 Sellers applied for an SBA Economic Injury Disaster Loan (EIDL) in July 2020 and “falsely and fraudulently represented that he was authorized by ASMBC” to do so. He claimed the money would be used “solely as working capital to alleviate economic injury caused by [the COVID-19] disaster.”
 Instead, federal prosecutors allege that after the nonprofit received the $20,000 in EIDL money, Sellers used it for personal purchases, including $11,286.75 in credit card payments and approximately $1,000 toward his mother’s water bill.
 According to the indictment, ASMBC’s president emailed the SBA on Jan. 12, 2024, after learning of the loan, writing in part, “...I was not aware of nor did I approve the application for an Economic Injury Disaster Loan” and “In checking with the executive board of the convention they did not authorize any such application either.” The president wrote that Sellers was “the sole person” with access to the 501c3 account and had “surreptitiously applied for and received the loan and used the funds without any notification or authorization from the president or executive board.”
 The president of the Alabama State Missionary Baptist Convention emailed the SBA in January 2024 saying he "was not aware of nor did I approve" a federal disaster loan taken out in the convention's name, according to the indictment. (U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Alabama) Sellers also applied for and received money from the State of Alabama’s Nonprofit Organization COVID-19 Relief Grant Program, and according to the indictment, wrote in the application for funds that he would use the money to “ensure that our staff can continue to receive their compensations” [sic].
 In an application for the State of Alabama’s Revive Plus COVID-19 Relief Grant Program, prosecutors said Sellers claimed ASMBC had 10 employees, although in the application for EIDL he claimed there were 5 employees.
 After Sellers applied for the Revive Plus grant, prosecutors said ASMBC’s president applied for help but was denied because the fund “had already been exhausted by prior applications (including SELLERS’ unauthorized application).”
 Sellers also received $50,000 from an unnamed non-profit for “COVID-19 Emergency Response,” according to the indictment.
 Sellers is accused of spending $8,621.13 at two universities for two of his daughters, $5,654.61 to a home equity line of credit taken out in his mother’s name on his home, and $26,165.55 in car payments, in money meant for ASMBC 501(c)(3).
 Project Zion, INC 
 The indictment alleges Sellers also applied for state and federal COVID relief funds for non-profit Project Zion, Inc., and “fraudulently” reported that it had 10 employees, and that the money would be used to “cover partial payroll and cover expenses due to the affects [sic] of covid 19.” Prosecutors said he received $20,000 from the State of Alabama in Dec. 2020, and $50,000 from the same unnamed non-profit that awarded ASMBC 501(c)(3) money.
 Prosecutors said Sellers used some of that money to pay for his daughter’s undergraduate tuition, meal plan, and other university fees.
 In an application for an EIDL, Sellers claimed Project Zion had seven employees, three fewer than previously claimed.
 Prosecutors said money from Project Zion’s bank account was used on mortgage payments, and on the same home equity line of credit taken out in his mother’s name on his home.
 Sellers Lawn Care PPP loan 
 Federal prosecutors allege Sellers obtained a $20,415 COVID-19 relief loan by claiming a lawn care business had generated $98,000 in income and that he had reported it to the IRS.
 The indictment describes Sellers Lawn Care as a fictitious business. Prosecutors said Sellers applied for the Paycheck Protection Program loan through an Arizona-based lender in 2021, listing himself as the contact and submitting a selfie to verify his identity.
 A "selfie" Patrick Sellers submitted to verify his identity on a Paycheck Protection Program application for "Sellers Lawn Care," according to the federal indictment. (U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Alabama) According to the indictment, the application claimed the business earned $98,000 in gross income in 2020 and that Sellers had reported the income on a Schedule C, the federal tax form used to report profit or loss from a sole proprietorship.
 Prosecutors said Sellers submitted a purported copy of a 2020 Schedule C with the application. IRS records cited in the indictment showed no Schedule C filing by Sellers for that tax year.
 The lender approved the loan and deposited $20,415 into Sellers’ personal credit union account, prosecutors allege. The indictment does not identify the lender or the credit union by name.
